extracted.intended_audience: graduate students and readers learning algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Foundations / 'The Rising Sea')
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter (exposition + exercises) on completions, singularity types (nodes, cusps, tacnodes, ordinary m-fold points), the Theorem on Formal Functions, and several foundational results (Zariski Connectedness, Stein factorization, Zariski's Main Theorem, Castelnuovo's criterion). Contains definitions, theorem statements, proof sketches, and exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stronger form of the ideal-theoretic criterion for flatness
rubrics_metrics.description: An A-module M is flat if and only if for all finitely generated ideals I, the natural map I ⊗_A M → (?) is an injection. (Text: 'Show that an A-module M is flat if and only if for all finitely generated ideals I, the natural map I ⊗_A M is an injection.')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: if there is a counterexample for an ideal J that is not finitely generated, use it to find another counterexample for a finitely generated ideal I. The result reduces checking flatness to finitely generated ideals; used in the chapter to deduce flatness after completion by checking finitely generated ideals and using parts (b) and (c) of Theorem 29.2.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a node (curve singularity)
rubrics_metrics.description: X has a node at p if the completion of O_{X,p} at m_{X,p} is isomorphic (as topological rings) to k[[x,y]]/(xy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition uses completions; for varieties over non-algebraically-closed fields one may base change to the closure or distinguish 'split' vs 'non-split' nodes. Exercises illustrate checking this definition for concrete plane curve equations (e.g., y^2 = x^2 + x^3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of cusp, tacnode, triple point, ordinary m-fold point
rubrics_metrics.description: Over an algebraically closed field (char k ≠ 2,3): X has a cusp (resp. tacnode, triple point) at p if ^O_{X,p} ≅ completion of Spec k[x,y]/(y^2−x^3) (resp. (y^2−x^4), (y^3−x^3)). X has an ordinary m-fold point if ^O_{X,p} ≅ completion of Spec k[x,y]/(f(x,y)) where f is homogeneous of degree m with no repeated roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These singularity types are defined via isomorphism of completions with model singularities. The ordinary 2-fold point is a node; ordinary 3-fold point is a triple point. Exercises point to further ADE singularities (A_n, D_n, E6, E7, E8).

rubrics_metrics.name: δ-invariant (contribution to genus)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a curve singularity, the contribution it makes to the arithmetic genus — the difference between the genus of the curve and that of its normalization (for projective curves) — is called the δ-invariant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: δ(node)=1, δ(cusp)=1, δ(tacnode)=2. Exercises show δ>0 for any non-smooth singularity and give bounds (e.g., a reduced irreducible degree d plane curve can have at most (d−1)(d−2)/2 singularities of certain types).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of completions to study singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Singularities are best defined in terms of completions: many singularity types (nodes, cusps, tacnodes, etc.) are determined by the completed local ring ^O_{X,p}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasizes working on the 'formal model' via completions (completion is flat, blowing up commutes with flat base change) to analyze local behavior and to perform calculations (e.g., blow-up of a node).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Theorem on Formal Functions (29.4.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π: X → Y is a proper morphism of locally Noetherian schemes and F is a coherent sheaf on X. For q ∈ Y (closed point case presented), the completion of (R^i π_* F)_q at m_{Y,q} is canonically isomorphic to lim_n H^i(X_n, F|_{X_n}), where X_n is the nth infinitesimal neighborhood (thickening) of the fiber over q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formally: (R^i π_* F)^∧_q ≅ lim_n H^i(X_n, F|_{X_n}). Warning: this does not imply the finite-level base-change maps H^i(X_B, F)/m^n → H^i(X_n, F|_{X_n}) are isomorphisms for finite n. The proof is postponed; several important applications are given (Zariski's Connectedness Lemma, Stein factorization, Zariski's Main Theorem, Castelnuovo's Criterion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and role of formal neighborhoods / thickenings
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z ⊂ W is cut out by ideal sheaf I, the closed subscheme cut out by I^{n+1} is the nth order formal (infinitesimal) neighborhood of Z in W. The 'formal neighborhood' refers to data of all such neighborhoods, often as an inverse limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the geometric input used to form the inverse systems whose limits appear in the Theorem on Formal Functions; computations may be done on affine neighborhoods and the system is cofinal with other natural systems (exercises illustrate these manipulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski's Connectedness Lemma (29.5.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y is a proper morphism of locally Noetherian schemes that is O-connected (see §26.1.7), then for every q ∈ Y the fiber π^{-1}(q) is connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses idempotents detected in completions: idempotents on formal neighborhoods lift to the completion ^O_{Y,q}, which is local, yielding a contradiction if the fiber were disconnected. The lemma is used repeatedly (e.g., in Stein factorization and birational contraction uniqueness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stein factorization (29.5.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any proper morphism π: X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes factors as X —α→ Y' —β→ Y where α has O-connected fibers (π_* O_X = α_* O_X makes Y' := Spec π_* O_X) and β is finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: Y' := Spec π_* O_X (a finite Y-scheme by coherence). α is proper and O-connected; β is finite. The factorization contracts the continuous parts of fibers. The theorem's construction is canonical and used in proofs of Zariski's Main Theorem and related results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness of contractions (exercise/criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: If π: X → Y and π': X → Y' are proper morphisms of locally Noetherian schemes, each contracting the same connected set of X (and both are isomorphisms elsewhere), and Y, Y' are normal, then π and π' are the same (there is isomorphism i: Y ≅ Y' with π' = i ◦ π).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal translation: the target of a contraction is determined by the locus contracted in X when the targets are normal. Hint: identify Y and Y' topologically and recover structure sheaves via Stein factorization/π_* O_X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolution of singularities of projective curves by blowing up
rubrics_metrics.description: For a reduced projective curve C over a field k, one can resolve singularities by repeatedly blowing up singular points; the process terminates because an integer invariant (arithmetic genus) strictly decreases when resolving certain singularities (e.g., resolving a node reduces pa by 1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategy requires showing (i) if pa(C) = pa(˜C) then C is already nonsingular; (ii) for any birational C' → C, pa(C') ≥ pa(C); (iii) blowing up a singular point decreases pa. The text explains how to use cokernels supported at finite sets, exact sequences, and the behavior of χ to control pa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zariski's Main Theorem (Grothendieck's form, 29.6.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose π: X → Y is a proper morphism of locally Noetherian schemes. (a) The set X_0 of points of X that are isolated in their fiber is open. (b) The restriction π|_{X_0}: X_0 → Y factors as an open embedding X_0 ↪ Y' followed by a finite morphism Y' → Y.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theorem yields a canonical factorization for the locus of points which are isolated in their fibers; the proof reduces via Stein factorization and identifies X_0 with the unramified locus (where Ω_{α}=0). Several variants and generalizations are discussed (e.g., relaxing Noetherian hypotheses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of finite morphisms (29.6.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a morphism π: X → Y of locally Noetherian schemes, the following are equivalent: (a) π is finite; (b) π is affine and proper; (c) π is proper and quasi-finite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketch of implications: finite ⇒ affine+proper by definition and Proposition; affine+proper ⇒ proper and finite fibers (quasi-finite); proper+quasi-finite ⇒ finite via Zariski's Main Theorem producing a finite factorization and checking X = X_0 so the finite part covers all of X.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completion of a Noetherian local ring is local (29.5.A)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (A,m) is a Noetherian local ring then its completion ^A := lim A/m^n is a local ring with maximal ideal m ^A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: show any element not in m ^A is invertible. This foundational fact is used repeatedly (e.g., in the proof of Zariski's Connectedness Lemma via idempotents in ^O_{Y,q}).

rubrics_metrics.name: Castelnuovo's Criterion for contracting (−1)-curves (29.7.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let C be a (−1)-curve on a smooth projective surface X over k. Then there exists a birational morphism π: X → Y with Y a smooth projective surface, π(C) a k-point, π is the blow-up of Y at that point, and C is the exceptional divisor of the blow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof strategy in three steps: (1) construct an invertible sheaf L (complete linear series) that is base-point-free and whose map contracts C to a point; (2) use the Theorem on Formal Functions to show the image Y is smooth at the contraction point by analyzing the inverse limit of H^0 on infinitesimal neighborhoods; (3) recognize π as the blow-up using the universal property. Many exercises guide the construction (vanishing, base-point-freeness, normalization, ring computations on thickenings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Blow-up of a node: local description of exceptional divisor (exercise 29.3.D)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X has a node at p, then the blow-up of X at p yields a morphism β: ˜X → X where the exceptional divisor β^{-1}(p) consists of two reduced smooth points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hint: use that completion is flat and that blowing up commutes with flat base change; reduce to computing the blow-up of the formal model Spec k[[x,y]]/(xy). This illustrates how node singularities resolve under a single blow-up.
